name: Coarctation

question.stem: A 1-day-old boy in the newborn nursery is noted to have cyanosis of his legs, but his arms are pink and well-perfused. Pulse oximetry demonstrates an oxygen saturation of 96% in the right arm and 65% in the right leg. An echocardiogram reveals an area of narrowing within the lumen of the proximal descending thoracic aorta.
question.prompt: Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention at this time?

explanation.text: This newborn presents with differential cyanosis, characterized by normal oxygen saturation in the right upper extremity (preductal) much higher than that in the lower extremity (postductal). This pattern reflects right-to-left shunting across a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), allowing deoxygenated blood to preferentially enter the descending aorta distal to the obstruction. This finding strongly suggests a ductal-dependent systemic circulation due to critical coarctation of the aorta (CoA), as confirmed by this patient’s echocardiogram. In neonates with critical CoA, closure of the ductus arteriosus results in markedly decreased perfusion to the lower body and can rapidly lead to cardiovascular collapse. Therefore, the most important immediate management step is to administer prostaglandin E1 to restore or maintain ductal patency and ensure adequate systemic blood flow distal to the obstruction. This intervention stabilizes the patient and improves systemic perfusion until definitive repair can be performed.

Surgical repair is the definitive treatment for CoA and is typically performed after stabilization with prostaglandin E1 and inotropic support. It is preferred over catheter-based approaches in neonates and very young infants due to a lower risk of reintervention.

Balloon angioplasty, often with stent placement, is more commonly used in older children or for the management of recoarctation after surgical repair. In neonates, it is generally reserved for select cases in which surgery is not feasible or as a temporizing measure.

Furosemide is indicated in patients with heart failure symptoms due to volume overload, but it does not address the underlying pathophysiology of ductal-dependent systemic blood flow in critical coarctation. In this scenario, it would not improve lower extremity perfusion or correct the cyanosis.

Indomethacin promotes closure of the ductus arteriosus and is used for conditions such as persistent PDA. In this patient, closure of the ductus would eliminate the compensatory shunt and precipitate heart failure and cardiovascular collapse.

testingPoint: Recall that the most important initial step in the treatment of critical coarctation of the aorta (CoA) in a neonate is administration of prostaglandin E1, to maintain patency of the ductus arteriosus. This ensures adequate systemic blood flow distal to the aortic obstruction.
